title: Never Stop Driving #197: Woodward Dream Cruise, a Goodyear Blimp ride, and an 810-hp Mustang

body_markdown:
Last week I climbed aboard *Wingfoot Two,* one of Goodyear’s three American airships, for a bird’s-eye view of the[Woodward Dream Cruise.](https://www.hagerty.com/media/events/woodward-dream-cruise-celebrating-what-we-do-in-detroit/) The blimp ride sent me down a rabbit hole, and what I found is worth sharing.


First, a correction. *Wingfoot Two* is not technically a blimp because it’s more than a helium-filled balloon. An internal frame retains the vessel’s shape, so it’s known as a rigid airship. The airship concept was famously pioneered by German pilot Ferdinand von Zeppelin; the[company he founded](https://www.zeppelin.com/de/en/) in 1908 still exists and manufactured Goodyear’s latest airships about a decade ago.


Cameron Neveu


Stretching 246 feet and weighing 10 tons, *Wingfoot Two* is maneuvered by three swiveling motors, one on each side and another on the tail. The carbon-fiber gondola’s massive windows provide massive views. The ship climbed quite aggressively from its mooring at Oakland County airport, north of Detroit, but then leveled off at 1000 feet and did a loop around the city of Pontiac, the northern terminus of the Woodward Dream Cruise. It was an amazingly serene experience.


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


Inside the helium envelope are air-filled bags called ballonets—one fore, one aft—that do two jobs simultaneously. As the airship climbs and helium expands, air is vented from the ballonets to prevent over-pressurization. On descent, a blower pumps air back in to maintain shape. But they also control pitch: Shifting air between the nose and tail ballonets trims the airship up or down, like a submarine managing its ballast tanks. The pilot explained all of this during the ride, and I realized that flying one of these things is unlike anything else in aviation. You’re not fighting gravity with speed the way an airplane does—you’re negotiating with buoyancy, constantly.


The pilots play a constant game of managing that buoyancy with ballast, and a critical source is the passengers. The 10 passengers are swapped, two at a time, to maintain the desired weight.


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


Docking and refueling after landing is a major production. A ground crew of about half a dozen follows the ship as it sways back and forth toward the ground, catching the ship and securing it to a mast. That mast is free rotating because even when on the ground, the airship moves with every puff of wind. One pilot called it the “world’s most expensive windsock.” The ground crew of some 20 people and several tractor trailers go wherever the airships go—about 100 events per year spread across Goodyear’s three vessels.


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


The pilots themselves are a fascinating fraternity. Most started as commercial airline pilots and were trained by veteran Goodyear pilots. There is no formal school to learn how to fly an airship. Goodyear has an internal department that runs its airship operations with a blimp-sized hangar near the company’s Akron, Ohio, headquarters.


CEO Mark Stewart is restructuring Goodyear toward premium products.[During the company’s most recent earnings call](https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-goodyear-tire-posts-q2-2026-revenue-beat-as-shares-fall-93CH-4842733) , he noted that the percentage of 18-inch and larger tires, which are considered premium products, in Goodyear’s product mix grew by four percentage points, the fastest pace of expansion since Goodyear began tracking the metric. Premium tires for premium vehicles, backed by a premium brand. The blimp operation, which costs tens of millions per year to operate, reinforces the marketing plan.


And it always has. The program has run for 100 years, covering more than 2500 events and carrying over 500,000 passengers. Rapper Ice Cube understood its cultural power: In his 1993 song “It Was a Good Day,” he described his perfect 24 hours culminating with the Goodyear Blimp displaying his name. The song became a classic, the lyrics became famous, and last year during the BIG3 basketball tournament, Goodyear finally made it literal, flying with the message “Ice Cube’s A Pimp” above Orlando.


Eddy Eckart


As for the Dream Cruise, the world’s largest single-day car event didn’t disappoint. Its scale is just incredible, with the heart of the Cruise stretching along 10 miles of Woodward Avenue between the Detroit suburbs of Ferndale and Birmingham. Over a million people attend with tens of thousands of cars. It is an automotive smorgasbord, a wonderful display of folks just having fun cruising in their favorite rides. From ratty Fox-body Mustangs to Ferraris to ’50s Caddies to lowriders to microcars, I saw seemingly one of everything and an endless assortment of characters, like a gray-haired dude popping wheelies on a tiny Honda Z50 minibike. The Cruise’s vibe is that everyone loves cars and whatever you are into, bring it. There is nothing else like it.


Timed to the Dream Cruise, Goodyear opened the Motor City Garage, its first enthusiast-concept retail store, at 3075 East Grand Blvd. in Detroit. The facility is modeled on the idea of a Starbucks Reserve Roastery or Nike House of Innovation and is a gathering place for car people, not just a tire shop, with displays that showcase Goodyear’s products, technology, and its history in Detroit going back to Henry Ford’s 999 race car in 1901.


Goodyear


At Ford’s massive encampment along Woodward Avenue, I learned something that stopped me cold. Ford Performance[offers a dealer-installed supercharger kit for 2024-26 Mustang GT and Dark Horse models](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/factory-tuned-we-drive-fords-800-hp-mustang-700-hp-f-150-and-300-hp-maverick/) . The $10,500 kit—developed in partnership with Whipple Superchargers and engineered to Ford’s 100,000-mile durability standards—takes the Coyote 5.0 V-8 from 480 hp to 810, along with 615 lb-ft of torque. A base Mustang GT stickers at $46,560, so do the math: For roughly $60,000—less than the price of many crossover SUVs—you can have an 810-hp muscle car with a 3-year/36,000-mile Ford Racing Parts warranty, provided a dealer does the installation. A Ford engineer told me demand has been so strong that Ford is ramping up production of the Whipple blowers to keep pace.


I drove one of the supercharged Mustangs, which chirped its rear tires in the first three gears. What most impressed me was how intelligently the traction control managed it—letting the tires break loose just enough to feel the full force of 810 hp without letting the car get away from you. It’s a fine line, and the engineering calibration walks it well. The ’Stang also seamlessly idled along in Dream Cruise traffic.


Ford


Amazing. What a time we are in. Mustangs with 810 horsepower and a Detroit weekend where over a million people gather to celebrate their love of cars. Wow.

Larry
